transcript.speech: This button is an example of confirm shaming.
This is part 4 of my Dark Side of UX series, not to be confused with my Build for Good UX series,
where I show you the psychological tricks that are being played on you as a user of the web.
Confirm shaming is when the decline option is worded literally to shame you.
The whole goal is to emotionally manipulate you into doing something that you wouldn't have done otherwise.
So why are people falling for this? There's a paradigm from the 1990s
called 'Computers are Social Actors'.
This research came from Stanford and decades later, surprise surprise, it still holds up.
It found that people mindlessly apply social rules and expectations to computers,
even though that we know are machines with no feelings.
It's the same reason people will say thank you when they're just using a chatbot.
So even though this is just a button, your brain is reacting like this is a real person judging you.
This also creates cognitive dissonance.
You might be thinking 'I'm a smart person', but then clicking 'I hate saving money' don't fit.
And one of the easiest ways to remove that discomfort is to give in.
But you can only guilt someone so far. The second that you notice it,
that guilt turns into reactance. AKA you're not guilting me into this,
and now you just resent the brand.
Here's one example you might be familiar with: travel insurance.
Look at this language. They could have just had a button with 'No thanks.'
But instead it's 'No, I'm willing to risk my flight'.
Or this one where it lists out the price of the trip and then it uses language like 'only' for the travel insurance.
And also trying to add in all the what ifs of 'you could miss a connection', 'you could miss your flight'.
Follow for part 5.

visual_demonstrations.observation: A simulated web modal overlay pops up with two buttons: a primary accept button ('Yes! I'd like the discount') and a guilt-inducing decline button ('No thanks, I like full price'). A cursor clicks on the decline button.
visual_demonstrations.before: The presenter is speaking holding a mic.
visual_demonstrations.after: The cursor clicks the 'No thanks, I like full price' button in the modal graphics.

visual_demonstrations.observation: An airline flight checkout interface displaying flight insurance options via radio buttons. The decline option reads: 'No, I'm willing to risk my [blacked out] flight.'
visual_demonstrations.after: A second travel insurance UI example is displayed showing 'No, I will travel without this insurance for my $1,198.03 trip...'

creator_derived_lessons.creator_statement_paraphrase: Confirm shaming manipulates users emotionally by phrasing decline options in ways that induce guilt or shame, leading to user resentment.
creator_derived_lessons.visual_evidence: Examples of decline options shown include 'No thanks, I like full price', 'No thanks, I hate saving money', and 'No, I'm willing to risk my flight'.
creator_derived_lessons.ux_problem: Decline options in modals or checkouts are explicitly worded to induce guilt, shame, or cognitive dissonance in the user.
creator_derived_lessons.recommended_change: Replace shame-inducing wording on decline options with simple, neutral language.
creator_derived_lessons.specific_visual_or_interaction_change: Change decline button labels from guilt-inducing phrases like 'No, I'm willing to risk my flight' to a simple, neutral 'No thanks'.
creator_derived_lessons.creator_reasoning: When users recognize confirm shaming, the guilt turns into psychological reactance and brand resentment, destroying trust.
creator_derived_lessons.applicable_context: Web page popups, discount offers, newsletter signups, and checkout upsells like travel insurance.

analyst_interpretation.interpretation: The video highlights 'confirm shaming' as a dark pattern leveraged through psychological principles like the 'Computers as Social Actors' paradigm and cognitive dissonance. The creator argues that while it might push short-term conversions, it damages long-term brand equity due to psychological reactance.
inferences_not_shown_or_said: Exact conversion rate impact of neutral vs. confirm-shaming buttons is not provided.
